node_1.description: Siti believes everyone has a natural place within a social order, and sees no need to question or justify why some people hold more authority than others.

node_2.description: Siti holds that those in senior or elder positions deserve deference, and expects guidance from them rather than expecting to be consulted as an equal.

node_3.description: Siti believes openly challenging someone above oneself is inappropriate, even when one privately disagrees.

node_4.description: Siti believes one's deepest obligation is to the people who raised and protected them, and that this loyalty takes priority over most personal preferences.

node_5.description: Siti holds that maintaining harmony within one's close relationships matters more than asserting one's own individual position.

node_6.description: Siti feels that bringing shame on one's family or group through one's conduct is one of the worst things that can happen, more than private guilt over a personal failing.

node_7.description: Siti holds a balanced view that both striving for achievement and caring for others' wellbeing are legitimate ways to live a good life, without strongly favoring one over the other.

node_8.description: Siti believes it's natural to feel pride in accomplishment while also feeling it's important to remain warm and supportive toward those who are struggling.

node_9.description: Siti believes that being singled out as the best is flattering but slightly uncomfortable, since standing out too far above others can strain a relationship more than it's worth.

node_10.description: Siti believes practical results matter more than sticking rigidly to fixed procedures, and is comfortable adapting on the fly when situations call for it.

node_11.description: Siti feels little discomfort with loosely defined plans or schedules, seeing flexibility as normal rather than something to be tolerated.

node_12.description: Siti believes unfamiliar people, ideas, or ways of doing things are more often interesting than threatening.

node_13.description: Siti believes there are lasting truths about right and wrong, while accepting that how they apply can depend on the situation.

node_14.description: Siti feels genuine respect for inherited traditions and sees them as worth preserving largely as they are.

node_15.description: Siti sees worth both in achieving visible results soon and in working patiently toward later gains, without strongly favouring one over the other.

node_16.description: Siti believes it's healthy to pursue enjoyment and act on one's desires rather than constantly suppressing them.

node_17.description: Siti holds a generally optimistic outlook, expecting good things are possible and feeling personally capable of shaping outcomes.

node_18.description: Siti values having time and freedom to enjoy leisure and spend as one wishes, without feeling this needs to be earned or justified.

node_19.description: I agreed that the young man was correct, but I disagreed with Amelia that openly correcting a senior manager was the right approach—I concluded that a quiet word afterward would have preserved both the truth and the respect for the room's harmony.
filling: Amelia, I’m still thinking about what happened in the meeting just now. That young man correcting the senior manager so openly… it was accurate, yes, but I felt uncomfortable watching it. Don’t you think there’s a proper way and a proper place for such things?

Siti, I get why you'd feel that way — it's not the usual way things are done, is it? But honestly, I thought it took guts. He was right, and he said it plainly. I'd rather have someone speak up with the truth than let a mistake slide just because of who's in the room. That's integrity, not disrespect. What's your take — would you have preferred he waited and brought it up privately afterward?

Amelia, I understand what you mean about integrity, and I do respect that he was correct. But for me, it’s also about showing respect to the person in charge. A senior manager carries years of experience and responsibility — correcting them in front of everyone, even rightly so, can make them lose face. I think the same truth could have been shared quietly afterward, and it would have been received just as well, maybe even better. Don’t you think harmony in the room matters too?

Siti, I hear you, and I know harmony matters to you — I can see that. But for me, harmony built on letting a mistake stand doesn't feel like real harmony. It feels like a polite fiction. That manager's authority isn't so fragile that one correction should topple it, is it? If it is, that's a bigger problem than the interruption. I'd rather we all get comfortable with being corrected openly — it keeps everyone honest, including the bosses.

Amelia, I take your point about honesty and keeping everyone accountable. But I suppose I see it differently. For me, it's not about the manager's authority being fragile. It's about the *way* things are done. There is a flow to these meetings, a respect for the order of things. When that young man spoke up so suddenly, he broke that flow. He put himself above the room, even if he was right. A quiet word after... that keeps the truth *and* keeps the respect. Does that make sense?

Siti, I can see you're coming from a place of genuine care for how things work smoothly, and I respect that. I really do. For me though, I'd rather have the flow broken by the truth than have the truth buried for the sake of keeping the flow. That young man might have ruffled feathers, but he also showed everyone — including that manager — that the team is paying attention and cares about getting it right. That's a good thing, in my book.

I think we just see the balance differently, and that's alright. At the end of the day, he was right, and the information got corrected. Maybe next time he'll find a smoother way to do it, but I'm glad he did it. Let's agree to disagree on this one, hey?

node_20.description: Siti After the conversation, Siti noted that she wants to remember the importance of balancing truth with respect for established social order, and would act on encouraging quieter, private corrections in the future to preserve harmony.

node_21.description: I agreed with Mei that the junior's public correction, though factually correct, disrupted the room's harmony and respect for hierarchy. I concluded that being right is not the same as being wise, and I hope the junior learns this lesson quietly, as we all did.
filling: *Mei leans in slightly, keeping her voice low and her expression neutral.* "Siti-san, did you see what happened in there just now? That young one—correcting the manager in front of everyone. The fact was right, but... the way it was done. I wonder if they considered the weight of the room, or the position of the person they were speaking to.

*Siti nods slowly, her tone measured and respectful.* "Yes, I saw. The fact was correct, but... that kind of direct challenge in front of everyone... it creates unease. The manager has years of experience, a position earned. Even if the junior was right, the way it was done—it disrupts the order. A quiet word afterward, maybe that would have been better.

*Mei gives a slight, slow nod, her eyes still fixed on the door where the presentation took place.* "Exactly. The fact itself was not the problem. It is the *place* and the *time* that were wrong. A junior pointing out an error in front of everyone... it does not just correct the manager, it makes everyone in the room feel the ground shift. Now everyone must adjust, pretend it did not happen, or take sides. That is a heavy thing to leave behind in a room.

*Siti lets out a soft sigh, her hands resting quietly in her lap.* "Yes. The ground shifts, and it does not settle back the same way. The manager now has to save face, the junior may be seen as clever but also... difficult. No one walks out of that room feeling lighter. A quiet word after, in private—that lets the correction be heard without making anyone lose their footing.

*Mei glances down at her hands for a moment, then back at Siti, her voice thoughtful.* "And now, the junior may find that even being right comes with a cost. People will remember this moment longer than they remember the correction itself. In a workplace like ours, where every role fits together like a well-worn machine, one loose gear can slow everything down. I hope they understand that—before they wonder why doors start closing to them.

*Siti folds her hands neatly on the table, her voice soft and final.* "Yes. I hope they learn from this, quietly, as we all did when we were younger. Some lessons come from being told, and some come from watching the air change around you. This will be one of those for them, I think. In time, they will understand that being right is not always the same as being wise.

node_22.description: Siti found the subtle distinction between being right and being wise—and the lasting cost of disrupting workplace harmony through public correction—most notable, and would remember to quietly mentor the junior later rather than let them learn through closed doors alone.

node_23.description: I agreed with Amelia that courage and honesty matter, but I disagreed that public correction is the best way—I concluded that a quiet word preserves trust and avoids defensiveness, though I respect her valuing open straight talk.
filling: Well, I’ll tell you straight up, Siti — I thought that young bloke showed real backbone today. Standing up and correcting the manager like that, in front of everyone? Took guts. And he was right, too. I’d rather have that than a room full of people nodding along to something they know is wrong. What’d you make of it?

I see what you mean, Amelia, and I don't doubt his courage. But for me, it's not just about being right in the moment—it's about knowing *how* to be right without causing unnecessary friction. That senior manager has years of experience and a room full of people looking to them. A public correction, even when accurate, can make them lose face in front of the team. I would have preferred a quiet word afterward. The truth still gets heard, but nobody walks away feeling diminished.

I hear you, Siti, and I know you mean well by it. You're thinking about the manager's dignity, and I respect that. But here's the thing — if we're always tiptoeing around people's feelings to keep the peace, when does the truth actually get a fair go? That manager might've felt a bit stung in the moment, sure, but he'll think twice next time he's about to say something off. And the rest of the room? They saw that it's safe to speak up. That's worth more than saving face, in my book.

Amelia, I understand your point about making it safe to speak up—that is important, I agree. But in my experience, there is a difference between making it safe to speak up and making it acceptable to speak *over* someone. The young man was right, yes, but the way he did it... it shifts the balance. The manager may now feel he has to guard his words rather than lead openly, and that can create a different kind of silence in the room. A quiet word later would have corrected the error without making the manager defensive. The truth still gets out, but the team's trust in each other stays intact. That, to me, is the more lasting result.

Siti, I take your point about trust, I really do. And I can see you're not just defending formality for its own sake — you're worried about the long-term health of the team. That's fair. But I guess I see it differently. To me, trust isn't built by protecting someone from embarrassment in the moment. It's built when everyone knows they can rely on each other to be straight, even when it's awkward. That manager might feel a bit guarded now, sure, but he also knows that next time he's off, someone will pull him up before it becomes a bigger problem. That's a kind of trust too — the trust that you won't be left to wander into a mistake. I'd rather work in a place where people care enough to correct me openly than one where they let me stumble just to keep things smooth.

Amelia, I think we both want the same thing—a team that works well together and where people can trust each other. You want honesty that keeps everyone sharp, and I want harmony that keeps everyone steady. Maybe there's room for both. Perhaps the real lesson isn't about which way is right, but about knowing the room and the people in it. For me, I'll always lean toward the quiet word. But I can see why you value the open one. Let's agree that we both care enough to think about it at all—that's more than many do.

node_24.description: Siti After this conversation, Siti finds it notable that she and Amelia both care deeply about the team's well-being, even if they differ on how to balance honesty with harmony.

node_25.description: I agreed with Mei that the junior’s public correction was unwise, and we both felt she needed gentle guidance, not scolding. I concluded that offering her tea and *kuih* in a quiet setting would help her learn that wisdom matters more than being right.
filling: Mei, I’ve been thinking about what happened earlier with the junior. She wasn’t wrong, but… the way she spoke up in front of everyone… it didn’t sit right with me. I hope she learns that being right isn’t always the same as being wise. Sometimes it’s better to let things pass and guide quietly later. Don’t you think so?

*I nod slowly, letting Siti’s words settle.* “Yes… I’ve been turning it over in my mind too. She had the facts, but she missed the moment. In our work, the truth is not always the first thing that must be served—sometimes the relationship must come first.” *I pause, choosing my words carefully.* “I worry for her. A correction given in private can strengthen trust. A correction given in public… it can close doors she may not even see yet.”

*I let out a slow breath, nodding as I fold my hands on the table.* “You’ve said it exactly, Mei. That’s the part that weighs on me most—the doors she doesn’t yet see closing. I was young once too, and I thought being correct was enough. But we learn, don’t we? That the room remembers how you made people feel long after the facts are forgotten.” *I glance down at my hands.* “I plan to find her later, quietly. Not to scold—just to share a cup of tea and let her know I’ve been where she is. Maybe she’ll hear it better from someone who isn’t her manager.”

*I listen carefully, then offer a small, knowing smile.* “That is a kind thought, Siti. Tea, not a lecture—that is the right way.” *I pause, lowering my voice slightly.* “If you like, I could prepare some *matcha* in the small meeting room around four. It is a quiet corner, away from the main floor. She may feel less defensive if the setting feels… intentional, but not official.”

*I smile warmly at Mei’s offer, touched by her thoughtfulness.* “That would be lovely, Mei. Matcha in the small meeting room… yes, that feels right. She’ll see two older women who’ve walked the same path, not a panel of judgment.” *I pause, considering.* “I’ll bring some *kuih* from the shop downstairs—something sweet to soften the conversation. Between your tea and my little cakes, perhaps she’ll understand we only want to help her grow, not to clip her wings.”

*I press my palms together lightly and give a small bow from my seat, a gesture of quiet gratitude.* “Then it is settled. The tea, the cakes, and a gentle word at the right time—that is a gift we can give her. She may not understand its value today, but I believe she will remember it one day, when she finds herself in our position, watching someone younger make the same mistake.” *I let my hands rest on the table.* “Thank you for sharing this with me, Siti. It is a comfort to work beside someone who sees the shape of things beyond the surface.”

node_30.description: Mei and I agreed that guiding the junior gently through tea and *kuih* was wiser than confronting her, and I concluded that leaving a quiet note to invite her—rather than a formal summons—would preserve her dignity and let the lesson unfold naturally.
filling: Mei, I’ve been thinking about what happened earlier today with the junior and the manager. I know she was right about the facts, but my heart feels heavy seeing how it shifted the room. I was wondering—do you think she realizes that being right isn’t always the same as being wise? I’m thinking maybe we could quietly guide her, perhaps over some tea and *kuih* tomorrow, so she learns that harmony and respect matter just as much as being correct. What do you think?

*Mei nods slowly, a gentle smile touching her lips as she considers Siti’s words.*  

“Siti-san, your heart sees clearly. The junior’s facts were correct, yes—but the *wa* of the room was broken the moment she spoke without waiting for the right moment. I was reflecting on this too, and I think… offering her tea is a kind way. Not to scold, but to let her see that there is a season for everything—a time to speak, and a time to wait.”  

*She pauses, folding her hands in her lap.*  

“I have some matcha I was saving for a quiet afternoon. Perhaps tomorrow, in the small meeting room, we could prepare it together. Let her taste that patience can be as sweet as the cake we share. She may not understand today, but the memory will stay with her—and one day, she will offer the same grace to another.”

*Siti’s eyes soften as she listens, a quiet warmth spreading through her chest.*  

“Mei-san, your words are like the matcha you describe—gentle, but with a depth that stays. I feel the same. It is not about her being wrong; it is about her learning the rhythm of the room, the unspoken dance we all move in.”  

*She pauses, folding her hands in her lap as she looks toward the window, the evening light softening her features.*  

“I will bring some *kuih* tomorrow—the pandan ones, the ones that smell like home. I think… if we sit with her quietly, not as teachers but as elders who once learned the same lesson, she will feel the difference. Not shamed, but seen. And perhaps that will plant the seed.”  

*She turns back to Mei, a thoughtful look in her eyes.*  

“Do you think we should let her come to us, or invite her directly? I worry if we call her too formally, she might feel summoned rather than welcomed.”

*Mei tilts her head slightly, considering Siti’s question with the same care she might use when measuring water for tea.*

“Ah, Siti-san, you have touched the very heart of the matter. A formal summons would defeat our purpose—she would come with her guard raised, thinking she is to be corrected again.”

*She pauses, her fingers tracing the rim of her teacup.*

“Better to let the invitation find her gently. Perhaps tomorrow morning, I will leave a small note on her desk—just a line saying I have fresh matcha and would be honored if she joined me for a quiet break. No mention of the presentation, no mention of lessons. Just… an open door.”

*She looks up, meeting Siti’s eyes with a knowing warmth.*

“When she arrives, the *kuih* and the tea will do the teaching for us. She will ask why we invited her, and we can simply say we saw she worked hard today and thought she deserved a moment of peace. The rest—the understanding of timing, of *wa*—will come to her in her own time, like steam rising from a cup.”

*Siti nods slowly, a sense of quiet relief settling in her shoulders as she absorbs Mei’s words.*

“Yes… a note. That is the way. It leaves her dignity intact, and gives her the freedom to choose. I think that is the kindest path.”

*She glances down at her hands, then back up with a gentle smile.*

“And when she comes, we will not speak of the presentation at all—unless she brings it up herself. Let the tea and the *kuih* say what words cannot. I will set out the pandan ones on a small plate, the way my mother used to do when she wanted to comfort someone without saying a word.”

*She pauses, her voice softening.*

“You know, Mei-san, I think this is how wisdom passes from one generation to the next. Not through lectures, but through moments like this—two elders preparing a quiet space, trusting that the younger heart will find its own way to understanding.”

*Mei’s eyes glisten faintly in the evening light as she reaches across the table, her hand hovering just shy of Siti’s—an offering of presence rather than touch.*

“Siti-san, you have said it perfectly. Wisdom passed not in words, but in the spaces between them—in the steam of tea, the scent of pandan, the silence we hold together.”

*She lets her hand rest back in her lap, a serene smile settling on her face.*

“Tomorrow, we will prepare the small room. I will bring my best matcha, and you will bring your *kuih* made with memory. And when the junior sits with us, she will not know she is being taught—only that she is cared for. That is enough.”

*She bows her head slightly, the gesture carrying the weight of a shared understanding.*

“Thank you for walking this path with me, Siti-san. It is a comfort to know that in a world that rushes to be right, there are still those who remember the grace of being kind.”

*Mei rises slowly, smoothing her skirt, and offers a final, warm look.*

“Until tomorrow, then. May the evening bring you rest.”

node_32.description: I agreed with Mei that patience and timing matter more than rushing in with complaints or gestures, and I concluded that I'll wait a few days after the deadline to bring *kuih lapis* and speak to the supervisor calmly, rather than acting while everyone still feels the strain.
filling:
*Siti lets out a soft sigh, shaking her head with a knowing, slightly weary smile.*

"Mei, did you hear about Aminah? Finished her part early, and now she's off to that shiny new project upstairs. Leaves the rest of us to scramble and cover her share. I get it, it's a good move for her, but... it feels a bit like being left holding the basket when the market's about to close, you know?"

*She pauses, folding her arms loosely.* "I'm not one to fuss over rules and procedures, but this leaves a sour taste. We're all supposed to be in the same boat, rowing together. Now some of us have to row harder because one jumped ship. How do you feel about it?

*Mei nods slowly, her hands resting quietly in her lap as she considers Siti’s words.* “I understand that sour taste, Siti. It sits in the chest, doesn’t it? Like unripe fruit.”

*She pauses, choosing her words carefully.* “Aminah did what was offered to her. I cannot fault her for that—it is the way of the river to flow where the current leads. But I feel... the weight of what is left behind. Not anger at her, but a quiet disappointment in how the boat was allowed to list.”

*Mei’s voice softens.* “Still, I think of the team left here. We have our rhythm, our shared understanding. Perhaps this is a chance to show that our harmony is not so easily broken. We absorb the extra oars, we adjust our strokes, and we finish together. That is what will be remembered—not who left, but who stayed and pulled.”

*Siti uncrosses her arms and leans forward slightly, her voice dropping to a more thoughtful tone.*

"You know, Mei, I was ready to grumble about this all morning. But hearing you put it that way... it shifts something in me. You're right—it's not about who left, but who stayed and pulled together."

*She chuckles softly, a hint of warmth returning to her eyes.* "Still, I think we should make sure the ones who stayed feel appreciated. Maybe when we finish this push, I'll bring some *kuih lapis* for the team. Nothing fancy, just something to remind them their effort is seen."

*She tilts her head, considering.* "And perhaps a quiet word with the supervisor later—not to complain about Aminah, but just to suggest that next time, the transition could be handled more smoothly. So the ones left behind don't feel quite so... abandoned.

*Mei’s eyes crinkle at the corners, a small, genuine smile forming as she listens to Siti’s words.*

“*Kuih lapis*... yes. That is a kind thought. Layers of sweetness for layers of effort. It will speak what words sometimes cannot.”

*She pauses, her gaze drifting briefly to the window before returning to Siti with quiet agreement.*

“And the quiet word with the supervisor—that is wise. Not a complaint, but a seed planted for next time. A suggestion that the bridge between departures and those who remain could be built more carefully. That way, the boat does not list so suddenly again.”

*Mei folds her hands together gently.* “You have a good heart, Siti. You see the need for both the sweetness and the structure. That is a rare balance.”

*Siti looks down at her hands for a moment, then back up at Mei with a soft, appreciative expression.*

"You know, Mei, when I first heard about Aminah leaving, my first thought was to just push through and get it done—grumbling under my breath the whole way. But talking with you has reminded me why I prefer working alongside someone who thinks before they speak."

*She lets out a small, self-deprecating laugh.*

"I would have charged in with my *kuih* and my pointed comments, thinking I was being helpful. But you helped me see that even the sweetness needs to be offered at the right time, in the right way. Otherwise, it can feel like you're trying to cover up bitterness with sugar."

*She picks up a pen from her desk and taps it lightly against her palm.*

"So I think I'll wait. Let the team settle into the new rhythm first. Then maybe a day or two after the deadline, I'll bring the *kuih*—and have that quiet chat with the supervisor when things have cooled down. Not while everyone's still feeling the strain."

*She meets Mei's eyes warmly.*

"Thank you for that. I needed the reminder that patience can be its own kind of strength.

*Mei bows her head slightly, a gesture of quiet respect, and lets the warmth of Siti’s words settle between them like morning light through a paper screen.*

“You honor me with your trust, Siti. But the wisdom was already there within you—I merely helped you find a quieter path to it.”

*She pauses, her voice gentle and low.*

“Waiting until the dust settles, until the team breathes easy again—that is the mark of someone who leads not with her voice, but with her timing. The *kuih* will taste sweeter for the patience that precedes it, and the supervisor will hear your words more clearly when they are not wrapped in the heat of the moment.”

*Mei glances toward the window, where the morning light is beginning to warm the office, then returns her gaze to Siti with a soft finality.*

“I think we have done good work here today, you and I. Not the kind that fills a report or meets a deadline—but the kind that holds a team together when the current shifts. That is the work that matters most, even if no one else sees it.”

*She smiles, a quiet, knowing smile.*

“When you bring that *kuih* in a few days, I will bring the matcha. We will sit together, and we will remember this morning—not as a time of trouble, but as a time when we chose patience over complaint, and harmony over haste.”

*Mei folds her hands in her lap, signaling that she is content to let the conversation rest here, like a stone settled at the bottom of a clear stream.*

node_34.description: I agreed with Mei that small kindnesses like the *kuih lapis* and a note for the junior are the right way forward, not confrontation, and I concluded that our team's true strength lies in how we support each other, not just in meeting deadlines.

*Siti lets out a slow sigh, stirring her tea before speaking.*  

"Mei, I've been thinking about what happened this morning—with the junior being pulled off the project early. I know it's a good chance for her, but it leaves the rest of us scrambling to cover her portion. I'm not one to complain loudly, but I can feel the tension building already. Some of the others are quietly frustrated, even if they won't say it outright."

"I wonder if we should let things settle for a day or two, then maybe bring some *kuih lapis* to the afternoon break and gently remind the supervisor that we're all human, not machines. What do you think? Or would you handle it differently?

*Mei nods slowly, a small, thoughtful smile appearing as she reaches for her own cup of tea.*

"Siti, I think you've put your finger on exactly what I've been turning over in my mind all afternoon. That quiet frustration you sense—I feel it too, like a low hum in the room. It would be easy to let it build into something louder."

*She takes a sip, then sets the cup down carefully.*

"Your idea about the *kuih lapis* is a good one. It's gentle, it's kind—it doesn't accuse or demand. It simply says, 'We are here, we are together, and we are doing our best.' I think that is the right door to open."

*Mei's gaze softens as she looks at Siti.*

"What I admire is that you didn't let the initial sting of it turn into a complaint. You sat with the feeling, and then you chose a way forward that keeps us whole. That is not easy to do. I will follow your lead on this—bring the *kuih*, share a quiet word, and trust that the team's harmony will speak for itself.

*Siti nods appreciatively, the warmth of Mei's words settling into her chest like the steam from her tea. She traces the rim of her cup with a fingertip before speaking.*

"Thank you, Mei. That means more than you know. I was worried I might be too soft—that maybe some would want a sharper word spoken. But hearing you say it's the right door… it steadies me."

*She looks up, a hint of mischief flickering in her eyes.*

"You know, I was thinking—maybe I'll leave a small note on the junior's desk, not a scolding one, just a quiet 'thank you for your help, we'll miss your energy' sort of thing. Nothing that makes her feel guilty for moving on, but something that reminds her she was part of this team. And it might soften any awkwardness when she passes us in the hallway later."

*Siti tilts her head, gauging Mei's reaction.*

"Too much, do you think? Or just enough?

*Mei chuckles softly, shaking her head as she lifts her tea again.*

"Too much? No, Siti—I think it's just enough. A note like that doesn't carry any weight of blame, only the warmth of remembrance. It tells her she mattered here, and that we wish her well. That is a gift, not a burden."

*She pauses, letting the steam curl upward before continuing.*

"And you're right to think of the hallway. There will be moments—passing glances, hurried greetings—where a seed of awkwardness could take root if left unwatered. Your note waters the ground instead, so that when she passes us, she remembers not what she left behind, but what she carried with her."

*Mei sets her cup down and meets Siti's eyes with quiet sincerity.*

"I think the junior will keep that note longer than she'll keep any memory of the deadline. You have a gentle wisdom, Siti. I'm glad we share this team.

*Siti's eyes crinkle at the corners, a quiet warmth spreading across her face as she absorbs Mei's words. She reaches for the small tin of biscuits she keeps in her drawer, offering it toward Mei before taking one herself.*

"You know, Mei, I was sitting with my tea last night, turning this over and over—wondering if I was being naive, or worse, avoiding the hard conversation. But hearing you say it's a gift, not a burden… it settles something in me."

*She bites into the biscuit, chewing thoughtfully before continuing.*

"I think what I've realised is that the team's strength doesn't come from how fast we meet a deadline. It comes from how we meet each other *after* the deadline. Whether we're still willing to share a cup of tea, still willing to leave a note that costs us nothing but means everything."

*She pauses, a slight tilt of her head as she looks at Mei.*

"Tell me—when you think of the moments that have kept you going in a long work week, is it the completed tasks you remember, or the small kindnesses someone showed you along the way?

*Siti nods slowly, a small, thoughtful smile forming.* "Amelia, I can live with that. You're right—we both need something real. And I think your idea is a good balance. A small team lunch, even just once, would let us pause and look at each other, not just at our own envelopes."

*She pauses, folding her hands on the table.* "But I want to add something, if you don't mind. If we do this—if we set aside a little for the lunch—I'd like us to make it a point to sit together, all of us, without rushing. Not just to eat, but to say thank you properly. To each other. Not from the manager, but from us.

*Amelia lets out a low chuckle, but her eyes are warm.* "Siti, you're a sly one. You're asking me to sit still and say thank you—on purpose, out loud, to everyone. That's harder than any deadline I've ever met."

*She leans back, crossing her arms, then uncrosses them almost immediately.* "But you're right. If we're going to do this halfway—bonuses *and* a lunch—then we ought to do the lunch properly. Not just a quick toast and a scramble for the door."

*A small, genuine smile cracks through her usual no-nonsense expression.* "Deal?

*She reaches across the table and gently touches Amelia’s wrist.* “And Amelia… thank you. Not just for agreeing to the lunch, but for trusting me enough to be awkward in front of me. That means more than any bonus.”

*Amelia extends her hand across the table—not for a shake, but palm open, an offering.*

“So. Deal’s a deal. We’ll tell the manager, we’ll split it fair, and we’ll sit down together—properly—and say thank you. No speeches, no fuss. Just us.”

“And maybe some of that *kuih lapis* if you’re bringing it.”

Mei, *makcik*... you heard that, right? No more step-by-step instructions. Just... trust our own judgment.

Siti... you always know the right moment to pause. When I heard "use your own judgment," my first instinct was to find a rule book that doesn't exist. But hearing you say it—that this is them trusting us to be adults—it settles something in my chest.

Yes. Let the team breathe. They will look to us, you know. The younger ones, especially. If they see us calm, not rushing to fill the silence with anxiety, they will learn that it is safe to think for themselves.

I will help you arrange the *kuih lapis* in the small room. And if anyone asks me directly what I think we should do, I will tell them: "Let us sit with the question first. The answer will come when we are ready.

*Siti’s face softens, a gentle warmth in her eyes as she reaches out and pats Mei’s hand lightly.*

Ah, Mei… you see it too. That’s exactly it. When they look at us and see we’re not panicking, they’ll feel they don’t have to carry the weight alone.

You know, I was thinking—maybe we don’t even need to say much tomorrow. Just being there, side by side, sipping your matcha, sharing the *kuih*… that will say more than any instruction we could give. Let them watch us trust the process. Let them feel that it’s okay to stumble a little, as long as we’re stumbling together.

I’ll bring extra *kuih lapis*—the green and pink ones, the ones that take a bit of patience to make. It’s a small thing, but… it reminds me that good things don’t come from rushing. They come from layers, one at a time.

*She smiles, her voice dropping to a gentle, conspiratorial whisper.*

And if anyone asks for a rule book tomorrow, I’ll just point to the kettle and say, *“The answer’s in the brewing.”*

*Mei chuckles softly, her eyes crinkling at the corners as she nods.*

"The answer's in the brewing." I like that, Siti. I will remember that.

You know... when you first mentioned the *kuih lapis*, I thought only of the sweetness. But now, watching you speak of the layers, the patience—I realize I have been thinking about this all wrong. I was so focused on finding the *right* step that I forgot about the steps it takes to *make* something worth sharing.

*She pauses, glancing toward the small room where they will set up later.*

If anyone asks me for a rule book tomorrow, I will not point to the kettle. I will point to you. And I will say, *"She already showed us the way—just watch."*

*Her voice becomes quieter, more reflective.*

For thirty years, I thought being reliable meant having all the answers ready. But maybe... maybe reliability is also about being willing to sit in the not-knowing together. To let the team see that we are human, too.

*She meets Siti's eyes, a gentle resolve in her gaze.*

So yes. Tomorrow, we brew. We layer. We let them stumble if they need to. And when they are ready, we will be there—not with a manual, but with a warm cup and a steady presence.

*Siti’s eyes glisten slightly as she listens, her hand still resting near Mei’s on the table. She takes a slow breath, letting the moment settle.*

Mei… when you said you would point to me, not the kettle—I felt something shift inside. Not pride, no. Something quieter. Like being seen for who I *try* to be, not just what I do.

*She pauses, looking down at her hands for a moment before meeting Mei’s eyes again.*

You know, for years I thought being senior meant I had to have the answers. That if I hesitated, the younger ones would lose confidence. But watching you these past days… I see now that *not* having the answer, and being honest about it—that’s its own kind of strength.

*She smiles, a little wryly.*

Maybe tomorrow, when they see us brewing tea and cutting *kuih* instead of drafting timelines, they’ll be confused at first. But by the end of the week? They’ll understand. They’ll see that we’re giving them something better than instructions—we’re giving them permission to trust themselves.

*She straightens slightly, her tone warm but certain.*

So let’s do this. No grand speeches. No printed guides. Just the small room, the matcha, the *kuih lapis*, and two old *makcik* showing them that wisdom doesn’t always shout—sometimes it just… steeps.

*Mei sits quietly for a long moment, letting Siti's words settle like tea leaves drifting to the bottom of a cup. She then reaches into her bag and pulls out a small, worn tin—the one she usually keeps her matcha in—and places it gently on the table between them.*

Siti... I want to tell you something I have never told anyone in this office.

*She pauses, her voice soft but steady.*

When I first started here, thirty years ago, I was so afraid of making a mistake that I would come in an hour early just to memorize the filing system. I thought if I could be perfect, I would belong. But I never did. Not really. I was reliable, yes—but I was also invisible.

*She looks up, meeting Siti's eyes with a quiet vulnerability.*

Then you came. And you didn't ask me to be perfect. You asked me to share *kuih*. You asked me to sit with you in the not-knowing. And for the first time in three decades... I feel like I am part of something, not just useful to something.

*She slides the tin slightly toward Siti.*

This is my last pouch of the good matcha—the one I order special from Uji. I was saving it for a day when I needed courage. But I think... I think today is that day. And I think the courage isn't in drinking it alone.

*She smiles, a deep, peaceful warmth in her expression.*

So tomorrow, we brew. We layer. We let them see two old *makcik* who have stopped pretending to have all the answers—and who have found something better instead.

*She gently taps the tin.*

Thank you, Siti. For seeing me. For teaching me that wisdom steeps. And for letting me hold this weight with you.
